question: With reference to the early financial structure of the Dutch East India Company (VOC) compared to the English East India Company (EIC) at their inception, which of the following statements is correct?
options: The VOC operated on a voyage-by-voyage capital liquidation basis until 1650, whereas the EIC started with a permanent capital setup in 1600.

The VOC was established with a large, permanent capital stock that was not liquidated after each voyage, whereas the early EIC operated on joint-stock voyages where capital was returned to investors after each venture.
Both companies started with a single unified permanent capital pool that remained locked in for the entire 17th century.
The EIC was funded entirely by state subsidies from Queen Elizabeth I, while the VOC depended entirely on merchant guilds without state charter.
explanation: At its inception in 1602, the VOC was structured with a permanent capital fund that was locked in for a ten-year period (later extended indefinitely), meaning capital was not liquidated and returned to shareholders after each voyage. In contrast, the early English East India Company (EIC) from 1601 to 1612 operated on separate, individual voyage syndicates (first to twelfth voyages) where capital and profits were distributed back to investors at the end of each voyage before a permanent joint-stock was finally established.
